We need retrosynthesis route with 1 reaction for target SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

Interpret: It's a bicyclic? Actually a cyclopentane fused? Let's decode: There's a phenyl attached to an exocyclic alkene (CH2= C(Ph) -). Then attached to chiral carbon bearing cyclopentane ring with OH and CF3 group attached to same carbon? Actually C@@H1[CH2][CH2][CH2][C@@]1(OH)C(F)(F)F. So a cyclopentane with a tertiary alcohol bearing CF3? The carbon bearing OH also attached to CF3? The template likely carbonyl-ene reaction: forward reaction is carbonyl-ene: carbonyl + alkene -> allylic alcohol (hydroxy). So retrosynthetic step: break the C-O bond to give a carbonyl (ketone) and an alkene (ene). So target is product of carbonyl-ene: we need precursor: a ketone (probably a cyclopentanone with CF3?) and an alkene (maybe the exocyclic alkene). The carbonyl-ene forms new C-C bond between alkene carbon and carbonyl carbon, moving hydrogen from allylic position to carbonyl oxygen forming OH.

Thus retrosynthesis: break the C-O bond to give a ketone: the carbon bearing OH becomes carbonyl (C=O) and the alkene becomes C=C unchanged? Actually in carbonyl-ene, the alkene double bond shifts to form new C-C bond and carbonyl becomes alcohol. So reverse: from product (allylic alcohol) we get a carbonyl (ketone) and an alkene (with allylic hydrogen). The product has a CF3 attached to carbon adjacent to OH? The carbon bearing OH also attached to CF3 and part of ring. In reverse, that carbon becomes carbonyl carbon (C=O) attached to CF3 and ring. So precursor: a cyclopentanone with CF3 at carbonyl carbon? That seems unusual: carbonyl carbon cannot have CF3 and be carbonyl? Actually carbonyl carbon is attached to two groups: one is CF3, other is the rest of ring. So a trifluoromethyl ketone (CF3-CO-...). So precursor: CF3-CO- (attached to cyclopentane). The other fragment is the alkene: CH2= C(Ph)- (maybe attached to carbonyl carbon after reaction). In reverse, the alkene is separate: CH2= C(Ph)-CH2? Wait the new C-C bond formed is between the alkene carbon (the one bearing the allylic hydrogen) and the carbonyl carbon. In product, the carbon bearing OH is attached to the alkene carbon (the exocyclic carbon). So the alkene fragment is CH2= C(Ph)- (the carbon attached to carbonyl carbon). So precursor alkene is CH2= C(Ph)- (maybe with a hydrogen at allylic position). Actually the allylic hydrogen is on the carbon adjacent to the double bond (the carbon that becomes attached to carbonyl). In product, that carbon is the one bearing OH and attached to CF3 and ring. So the alkene precursor is CH2= C(Ph)-CH2? Not exactly.

Simplify: Use template ID for carbonyl-ene. We need to find a template that matches product. Use search for functional_groups_broken: ["C-C double bonds","ketones"]; formed: ["aliphatic hydroxyls","five-membered rings"] gave empty. Maybe need to include "five-membered rings" broken? Actually forward reaction forms five-membered ring, so retrosynthesis breaks five-membered ring? Wait product has five-membered ring (cyclopentane). In forward, a five-membered ring is formed. So retrosynthesis would break that ring? Actually carbonyl-ene can be intramolecular forming a new C-C bond that creates a ring. So product has a new five-membered ring formed from a linear precursor. So retrosynthesis would open the ring to a linear precursor lacking that ring. So functional_groups_broken includes "five-membered rings". Let's try search with broken: ["C-C double bonds","ketones","five-membered rings"]; formed: ["aliphatic hydroxyls"]; limit 5.
